title: Are all GPA functions the same?
text:
A look at the results and the speed to obtain them from several Generalized Procrustes Analysis functions in R.





library(geomorph)

# make a latticed cube
vert <- 5
template <- expand.grid(1:vert, 1:vert, 1:vert)
colnames(template) <- c("x", "y", "z")

# add points for n specimens
n <- 50
LM <- LMlist <- lapply(seq_len(n), function(.){
  as.matrix(template + rnorm(length(template),
                   mean = 0, sd = 0.3))
})

LM <- simplify2array(LM)
plotAllSpecimens(LM)




system.time(GPA1 <- gpagen(LM, print.progress = FALSE))

   user  system elapsed 
  0.009   0.001   0.011 

plot(GPA1)




library(Morpho)
system.time(GPA2 <- ProcGPA(LM))

   user  system elapsed 
  0.039   0.001   0.040 

plotAllSpecimens(GPA2$rotated)




two.b.pls(GPA1$coords, GPA2$rotated, print.progress = FALSE)

Data in either A1 or A2 do not have names.  It is assumed data in both A1 and A2 are ordered the same.



Call:
two.b.pls(A1 = GPA1$coords, A2 = GPA2$rotated, print.progress = FALSE) 



r-PLS: 1

Effect Size (Z): 4.2461

P-value: 0.001

Based on 1000 random permutations


Although they seem perfectly correlated, you might notice by spinning the plots a slight difference in the scatter. With gpagen, the default is to project configurations into a space tanget to shape space. The procGPA function does not do this. So, gpagen scatter looks more planar and procGPA more hemispherical at each point. We can update this so they are the same.

system.time(GPA1 <- gpagen(LM, print.progress = FALSE, Proj = FALSE))

   user  system elapsed 
  0.004   0.000   0.005 

plot(GPA1)




two.b.pls(GPA1$coords, GPA2$rotated, print.progress = FALSE)

Data in either A1 or A2 do not have names.  It is assumed data in both A1 and A2 are ordered the same.



Call:
two.b.pls(A1 = GPA1$coords, A2 = GPA2$rotated, print.progress = FALSE) 



r-PLS: 1

Effect Size (Z): 4.2619

P-value: 0.001

Based on 1000 random permutations






Similar results
gpagen is faster





library(shapes)
system.time(GPA3 <- procGPA(LM))

   user  system elapsed 
  0.183   0.005   0.191 

plotAllSpecimens(GPA2$rotated)




two.b.pls(GPA1$coords, GPA3$rotated, print.progress = FALSE)

Data in either A1 or A2 do not have names.  It is assumed data in both A1 and A2 are ordered the same.



Call:
two.b.pls(A1 = GPA1$coords, A2 = GPA3$rotated, print.progress = FALSE) 



r-PLS: 1

Effect Size (Z): 4.2656

P-value: 0.001

Based on 1000 random permutations






Similar results.
gpagen is faster

system.time(GPA4 <- fgProcrustes(LMlist, tol = 0.0001))

title: Are all GPA functions the same?
text:
Simulated Examples for gpagen
Concerning computational efficiency in GPA, there are two “big data” attributes for which to be concerned with geometric morphometric (GM) data: wide data, which is a large number of landmarks (including semilandmarks); and long data, which is a large set of landmark configurations (specimens). These should be studied independently in comparative computational assessments, to determine if attempted optimization of analytical functions is successful only in certain regards. To generate data, we use an automated function, which generates a shape template that is a grid formed along \(x\) and \(y\) axes, with the height of points inversely associated with distance from center, creating a dome-like figure. The fraction of sliding semilandmarks and level of variation for isotropic random points applied to the template can also be varied. 

get.array <- function(grid.n, spec.n, sdev= 0.5, f.surf = 0.5){
  x <- seq(0:grid.n) - mean(seq(0:grid.n))
  coord.t <- as.data.frame(expand.grid(x, x))
  colnames(coord.t) <- c("x", "y")
  coord.t$z <- apply(coord.t, 1, function(y) 0.5*(sqrt(max(x)^2) - sqrt(sum(y^2))))
  surf <- which(coord.t$z > quantile(coord.t$z, 1- f.surf))
  fixed <- (1:nrow(coord.t))[-surf]
  npk <- length(as.matrix(coord.t))
  coords <- lapply(1:spec.n, function(.) coord.t + rnorm(npk, sd = sdev))
  dims <- dim(coords[[1]])
  coords <- array(unlist(coords), c(dims, spec.n))
  list(template = coord.t, 
       coords = coords, 
       surf = surf, fixed = fixed)
}

title: Are all GPA functions the same?
text:
Wide data example
Below is an example template of a dome from a \(32 \times 32\) grid, with 50% of the landmarks as sliders (shown in red), with 20 specimens, created with this function. 

ex1 <- get.array(32, 20, 0.3, 0.5)


Before GPA

colors <- rep(1, nrow(ex1$template))
colors[ex1$surf] <- 2
plotAllSpecimens(ex1$coords,
                 plot_param = list(mean.bg = colors))







After GPA

GPA1 <- gpagen(ex1$coords, surf = ex1$surf, max.iter = 2, print.progress = FALSE)

plot(GPA1, plot_param = list(mean.bg = colors))

title: Are all GPA functions the same?
text:
Now compare the two functions.
Note that the slider3d function arrests after 2 iterations, even if more are allowed, so the arguments are adjusted for comparability of results.

system.time(
  {slide <- slider3d(ex1$coords,
                   SMvector  = ex1$surf,
                   surp = ex1$surf,
                   mc.cores = 6,
                   iterations = 2,
                   silent = TRUE); 
  GPA2 <- ProcGPA(slide$dataslide)})

no surfaces specified - surface is approximated from point cloud


   user  system elapsed 
 13.418   7.657   6.100 

system.time(
  GPA1 <- gpagen(ex1$coords, 
                 surf = ex1$surf, 
                 max.iter = 2, 
                 Parallel = 6,
                 Proj = FALSE,
                 print.progress = FALSE))

   user  system elapsed 
  5.397   4.607   4.860 

two.b.pls(GPA1$coords, GPA2$rotated, print.progress = FALSE)

Data in either A1 or A2 do not have names.  It is assumed data in both A1 and A2 are ordered the same.



Call:
two.b.pls(A1 = GPA1$coords, A2 = GPA2$rotated, print.progress = FALSE) 



r-PLS: 0.994

Effect Size (Z): -0.6938

P-value: 0.373

Based on 1000 random permutations



Conclusions

Comparable results
gpagen is faster
Each function has many more arguments to control operations. The ProcGPA function has more arguments for specific sliding objectives.

title: Are all GPA functions the same?
text:
Long data example

ex2 <- get.array(5, 500, 0.1, 0.5)

Plot of just a few specimens:

colors <- rep(1, nrow(ex2$template))
colors[ex2$surf] <- 2
plotAllSpecimens(ex2$coords[,,1:20],
                 plot_param = list(mean.bg = colors))





Note that the slider3d function arrests after 3 iterations, even if more are allowed, so the arguments are adjusted for comparability of results.
Now let’s compare:

system.time(
  {slide <- slider3d(ex2$coords,
                   SMvector  = ex2$surf,
                   surp = ex2$surf,
                   mc.cores = 6,
                   iterations = 3,
                   silent = TRUE); 
  GPA2 <- ProcGPA(slide$dataslide)})

no surfaces specified - surface is approximated from point cloud


   user  system elapsed 
100.515  27.806  29.820 

system.time(
  GPA1 <- gpagen(ex2$coords, 
                 surf = ex2$surf, 
                 max.iter = 3, 
                 Parallel = 6,
                 Proj = FALSE,
                 print.progress = FALSE))

   user  system elapsed 
  1.331   0.727   0.480 

two.b.pls(GPA1$coords, GPA2$rotated, print.progress = FALSE)

Data in either A1 or A2 do not have names.  It is assumed data in both A1 and A2 are ordered the same.



Call:
two.b.pls(A1 = GPA1$coords, A2 = GPA2$rotated, print.progress = FALSE) 



r-PLS: 0.939

Effect Size (Z): 3.5146

P-value: 0.001

Based on 1000 random permutations

title: Are all GPA functions the same?
text:
Conclusions

Wowza!
Morpho::ProcGPA is optimized for wide data.
geomorph::gpagen is optimized for both wide and short data
